"""Layer 15 MLP unit 1664 (the down_proj component), as a rule about literal data in code.

What it responds to: the item boundaries of literal lists, dicts and call arguments
written inside brackets, e.g. the comma after a number in `append(x, 4, 5)`, the quote
after a colon in `{'name': "...`, and the digit or quote that opens the next item.
Prose and bracket-free text get 0, and so do words inside brackets.

The predictions are a small table of (this token kind, previous token kind) pairs,
read off the component's mean activation in those contexts. Scale is roughly the
activation's own (typical values 0.3 to 1.5; the rare spikes near 20-40 are not
predicted). It explains under 1% of the variance: most of the component's variance
is in sparse spikes that no local rule here predicts.
"""

READS = ()

OPEN, CLOSE = "([{", ")]}"

# (kind of this token, kind of the token before it) -> predicted activation, inside brackets
TABLE = {
    ("comma", "digit"): 1.3,
    ("quote", "colon"): 1.4,
    ("digit", "quote"): 1.2,
    ("space", "comma"): 1.1,
    ("quote", "comma"): 1.0,
    ("colon", "digit"): 0.7,
    ("space", "colon"): 0.7,
    ("colon", "word"): 0.6,
    ("digit", "comma"): 0.55,
    ("digit", "word"): 0.4,
    ("digit", "open"): 0.35,
    ("other", "digit"): 0.35,
    ("word", "quote"): 0.33,
    ("digit", "other"): 0.3,
    ("space", "digit"): 0.25,
}


def _kind(s):
    """A coarse class of one token's text."""
    t = s.strip()
    if t.isdigit():
        return "digit"
    if t == ",":
        return "comma"
    if t == "":
        return "space"
    if t == ":":
        return "colon"
    if t[:1] in "\"'`":
        return "quote"
    if any(c in OPEN for c in s):
        return "open"
    if any(c in CLOSE for c in s):
        return "close"
    if t.isalpha():
        return "word"
    return "other"


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # carry: (document, bracket depth, kind of the previous token), reset at each document start
    s = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    depth, prev = (0, "start") if carry is None or carry[0] != doc else carry[1:]
    kind = _kind(s)
    value = TABLE.get((kind, prev), 0.0) if depth > 0 else 0.0
    depth = max(0, depth + sum(c in OPEN for c in s) - sum(c in CLOSE for c in s))
    return (doc, depth, kind), value

"""Layer 15 MLP down-projection, component 1665: a diffuse, mostly unexplained readout.

What the component is: a rank-one piece of layer 15's down_proj. Its input is the MLP's
hidden vector h (6144 units); it reads x = h . v with v spread over many hidden units (its
largest weight is on unit 1665 itself, but the top 200 units carry only 42% of v's energy),
and writes x * ||u|| into the residual stream. Its activation is roughly Gaussian around a
small positive mean (0.043, std 0.285), with no sparse firing and CI near 0, so switching it
off barely changes the model's output.

What this program does: it predicts the component's average activation at every position.
It reads no token, no context and no upstream component.

Why this is the whole program: we looked for readable structure and found none that
generalises. Token identity, previous token, token class (digit, punctuation, space-prefixed
word, CJK, ...), and position in the document each explain ~0 of the variance on held-out
rows. A linear model on token-class features of the last three tokens explains 0.3%.
The best held-out token-lookup table (which would need ~3000 arbitrary token ids) explains
about 0.6%. Those tables are not worth their size, so this program keeps the mean.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

MEAN_ACTIVATION = 0.043
"""The component's mean activation over the eval rows."""


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    """Predict the component's mean activation at this position."""
    return carry, MEAN_ACTIVATION

"""Component p-82af68dd@100000/layers.15.mlp.down_proj:1666.

This component is, in effect, one hidden unit of layer 15's MLP (neuron 1666 of the 6144 that
feed down_proj): its activation is that unit's value times about 1.3. The unit is mostly
near zero, with rare large positive spikes (up to ~50) and small negative values.

Nothing simple predicts the spikes. What the data does show is a rough split by kind of token:
  - the first token of a document is about zero (the start of a document is quiet);
  - a word-internal piece of a split word (letters with no leading space, e.g. "ual", "ment")
    is somewhat more often positive than a word-initial token;
  - digits are slightly positive, newlines slightly negative.
This program predicts those group means and nothing more. On the eval rows its variance
explained is about 0.003 (correlation 0.06), so it is a weak description of the component.
Its e2e effect is close to switching the component off.
"""

import regex

READS = ()

WORD_PIECE = 0.12  # letters with no leading space: the continuation of a split word
DIGIT = 0.08  # a digit token
NEWLINE = -0.07  # a line break or run of spaces


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    if len(prefix.document_ids) < 2 or prefix.document_ids[-2] != prefix.document_ids[-1]:
        return carry, 0.0  # first token of a document: about zero
    t = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if regex.fullmatch(r"\p{L}+", t):
        return carry, WORD_PIECE if not t.startswith(" ") else 0.0
    if regex.fullmatch(r"\p{N}+", t):
        return carry, DIGIT
    if t[:1] in ("\n", "\r") or t.strip() == "" and "\n" in t:
        return carry, NEWLINE
    return carry, 0.0

"""Creative-work detector for layers.15.mlp.down_proj, component 1668.

What the component is: its input weight is mostly one MLP hidden unit of layer 15 (unit
1668, about two-thirds of its squared norm). That unit is SiLU(gate) * up, so the component
is large only when the unit's gate is open, and the sign of its activation follows "up".

What it responds to: text about creative works (novels, films, TV, albums, songs, stories,
comics) and their genres (comedy, drama, fantasy, horror). It is strongest on lowercase
work words in running prose (novel, story, comedy, movie, film, episode) and weaker on
words for a work's parts or sub-forms (plot, characters, chapter, sequel). Inside a
passage about such a work it also stays on for the ordinary words nearby (e.g. "based on",
"of", "by"), so the program adds a smaller amount for each work word earlier in the same
document within the last 40 tokens.

What this program does not capture: the sign. The real activation goes negative on many
tokens in the same kind of context, which this program does not model; it predicts only
positive values. Code, lists of names and other technical text sit near zero or below.
"""

READS = ()

# Words that name a creative work, its form or its genre, grouped by how strongly they
# drive the neuron in the sample (strong > mid > weak).
STRONG = frozenset(
    """
    comedy novel novels drama story stories fantasy movie film films manga fiction episode
    """.split()
) | {"小说", "故事", "电影", "漫画"}
MID = frozenset(
    """
    starring book books song songs directed screenplay poem poems horror album albums
    television tales series movies musical plot characters
    """.split()
)
WEAK = frozenset(
    """
    chapter chapters character debut written sequel adaptation soundtrack novelist author
    authors sitcom cast comic comics tv play plays theatre show shows opera tale anime
    episodes director
    """.split()
) | {"剧"}

WINDOW = 40  # earlier tokens of the same document that count as context
CAP = 3  # context saturates after this many work words


def work_weight(token_string):
    """How much this token itself points at a creative work: 4, 2, 1 or 0."""
    word = token_string.strip().lower()
    if word in STRONG:
        return 4.0
    if word in MID:
        return 2.0
    if word in WEAK:
        return 1.0
    return 0.0


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    t = prefix.position
    doc = prefix.document_ids[t]
    # Creative-work words in the same document within the last WINDOW tokens before this one.
    context = 0
    for j in range(max(0, t - WINDOW), t):
        if prefix.document_ids[j] == doc and work_weight(prefix.token_strings[j]) > 0:
            context += 1
    context = min(context, CAP)
    value = 0.03 + work_weight(prefix.token_strings[t]) + 0.3 * context
    return carry, float(value)

"""Layer 15 MLP unit 1669 (down_proj component 1669), read as a comparison detector.

This component is almost entirely hidden-unit 1669 of layer 15's MLP: its input
direction is that one unit, and its output direction promotes words like "match",
"corresponding", "appropriate" and "aligned". Its activation is mostly diffuse noise
(mean -0.02, spread about 0.35) with occasional large positive spikes. The spikes
come on tokens that state a comparison, a threshold or a requirement:

  - equality and ordering operators in code (==, !=, !==, >=, <=, and the Unicode
    forms ≤ ≥), which carry the largest values;
  - "than" right after a comparative ("less than", "larger than", "older than");
  - "exceed", "least", "appropriate", "correct", "match" in prose about limits and
    fitness.

This program predicts those token classes with a fixed bump above the component's
average activation (-0.024), and that average everywhere else. It does not model the
diffuse noise, and it does not model which comparisons fire strongly: on eval it
explains about 0.3-0.7% of the variance (correlation about 0.09), because most of the
variance is in the noise. The bumps were set roughly from the mean activation per token
class on about 20k training rows.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

# Equality, inequality and ordering operators that test a condition.
STRONG = {"==", "!=", "!==", ">=", "<=", "≤", "≥", "exceed", "exceeds"}
# Operators that fire only weakly on average ("<" and ">" are often not conditions).
WEAK = {"===", "≠", "<", ">"}
# Comparatives that make a following "than" a comparison.
COMPARATIVES = {"less", "more", "larger", "smaller", "greater", "fewer", "older", "younger", "later", "bigger"}
# Words about meeting a requirement or a limit.
CRITERIA = {"least", "appropriate", "correct", "match", "matches", "matching"}


# The component's average activation, which every other token predicts.
BASELINE = -0.024


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    """The component's activation at the newest token, from that token and the one before it."""
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip()
    same_document = len(prefix.document_ids) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]
    before = prefix.token_strings[-2].strip() if same_document else ""
    if token in STRONG:
        bump = 1.0
    elif token in WEAK:
        bump = 0.3
    elif token == "than":
        bump = 0.8 if before in COMPARATIVES else 0.3
    elif token in CRITERIA:
        bump = 0.4
    else:
        bump = 0.0
    return carry, BASELINE + bump

"""Layer 15 MLP down-projection component 1670 (p-82af68dd).

What it does, in plain terms: this component reads a mix of layer 15's MLP hidden units,
dominated by unit 1670, and writes a small amount back into the residual stream. Its
activation (about 0.3 in standard deviation, centred near 0) is only weakly tied to which
tokens are present. Token-identity tables, even large ones, explain only about 1-3% of its
variance on held-out text, and position in the document explains almost none. The
simple rules below are the surface patterns that show up on average, and they score about
0.3% of variance on eval; the model's own context (not reproduced here) carries the rest:

- markup that opens or closes a tool call or a thinking block (<tool_call>, </tool_call>,
  <think>, </think>) pushes the activation clearly negative (about -0.33 on average);
- a line break that follows sentence punctuation (".\\n", ":\\n\\n", "/\\n", ...) pushes it
  mildly positive (about +0.12);
- everything else sits near the component's average, about -0.02.

The program needs no state: it reads only the newest token.
"""

READS = ()

TAG_TOKENS = {"<tool_call>", "</tool_call>", "<think>", "</think>"}
TAG_VALUE = -0.33
BREAK_VALUE = 0.12
REST_VALUE = -0.02
PUNCT_END = (".", ":", "/", "。", "?", "!")


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    text = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if text in TAG_TOKENS:
        return carry, TAG_VALUE
    stripped = text.rstrip()
    if text.endswith("\n") and stripped.endswith(PUNCT_END):
        return carry, BREAK_VALUE
    return carry, REST_VALUE

"""Constant predictor for layers.15.mlp.down_proj component 1671.

This component is effectively inert: it is almost never important (CI ~ 0) and
switching it off changes the model's output by about 1e-6 nats. Its activation is
a small, diffuse signal: a linear read-out of the layer-15 MLP hidden state, whose
largest share is the hidden unit 1671 (correlation about 0.35), with noise-like
contributions from thousands of other units. None of this is predictable from the
token identity, token class, or position in the document: the best lookups explain
under 3% of its variance. So the program predicts the typical value everywhere.
"""

READS = ()

MEAN_ACTIVATION = 0.007  # the component's average activation on training text


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    return carry, MEAN_ACTIVATION

"""Evidence-reporting words in Qwen3-1.7B layer 15, MLP down_proj, component 1672.

What it does: this component goes negative where the text presents empirical evidence:
the verbs that say what a study, figure or census shows ("revealed", "suggests",
"indicate", "showed", "demonstrated"), and the nouns for the source of the evidence
("studies", "census", "experiments", "findings", "results"). It is most negative on the
verb itself and a little on the token after it. Shortly after a citation cue ("Fig.",
"Table", "according to", "based on", "shown in", "et al.", "see"), the punctuation and
"that"/"to" that lead into the cited finding are negative, and the other tokens a little.
Everywhere else the program predicts 0, close to the component's typical value.

This is a small lexical model. It explains only a little of the component's variance,
because most of its variance is not carried by any words: a model that looks only at the
tokens around a position peaks at about R^2 0.04 on held-out text.
"""

READS = ()

# Words for showing or reporting a finding, with a typical activation for each.
EVIDENCE_VERBS = {
    "revealed": -6.0, "reveals": -2.7, "reveal": -1.5,
    "suggest": -4.0, "suggests": -4.0, "suggested": -4.0, "suggesting": -3.5,
    "indicate": -3.5, "indicates": -3.5, "indicated": -3.5, "indicating": -3.0,
    "confirms": -3.5, "confirmed": -3.0,
    "showed": -3.2, "shows": -2.8, "show": -1.5, "showing": -1.2, "shown": -0.5,
    "demonstrated": -2.5, "demonstrate": -2.5, "demonstrates": -2.0,
    "says": -1.8, "said": -1.5, "reported": -1.5, "reports": -2.2, "report": -1.0,
    "argues": -2.0, "stated": -0.9, "concluded": -1.3, "found": -0.6, "finds": -0.5,
    "estimates": -1.2,
}

# Nouns for the source of evidence.
EVIDENCE_NOUNS = {
    "studies": -2.6, "study": -1.3, "census": -3.3, "experiments": -1.9,
    "findings": -1.6, "results": -1.0, "analysis": -1.0, "survey": -1.1,
    "research": -0.9, "evidence": -0.6, "data": -0.4,
}

EVIDENCE = {**EVIDENCE_VERBS, **EVIDENCE_NOUNS}

# Words that cite a figure, source or earlier passage; they open a citation window.
CITATION_CUES = {
    "fig", "figure", "table", "et", "al", "according", "based", "see", "shown",
    "described", "cir", "col", "eq",
}
CITATION_WINDOW = 8  # tokens after a citation cue

# Punctuation and connectives that lead into the cited finding.
LEAD_INTO_FINDING = {",", ")", "),", "that", "to"}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    t = prefix.position
    token = prefix.token_strings[t].strip()
    word = token.lower()
    if t == 0 or prefix.document_ids[t] != prefix.document_ids[t - 1]:
        last_own, since_cue = 0.0, 10**6  # a new document starts with no context
    else:
        last_own, since_cue = carry
    since_cue += 1

    own = EVIDENCE.get(word, 0.0)
    value = own + 0.5 * last_own  # the token after an evidence word carries half its value
    if since_cue <= CITATION_WINDOW:
        value += -1.5 if token in LEAD_INTO_FINDING else -0.3

    if word in CITATION_CUES:
        since_cue = 0
    return (own, since_cue), value

"""Activation of the layer-15 MLP down-projection component 1673.

This component is essentially inert: it almost never passes the causal-importance
threshold (0 of 10M tokens), and switching it off changes the model's predictions by
about 1e-6 nats. Its activation looks like noise with no clear token or context
concept: the best simple description is that it is near zero everywhere, with a small
negative dip over the first few tokens of each document, which decays with position.

The program tracks each token's position within its document (the count resets when
the document id changes) and predicts -0.14 * 0.7**(position-1) for positions 1 and
later, and 0 at a document's first token.
"""

READS = ()

START = -0.14  # mean activation at a document's second token
DECAY = 0.7  # per-token decay of that dip


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or doc != carry[0]:
        k = 0
    else:
        k = carry[1] + 1
    value = 0.0 if k == 0 else START * DECAY ** (k - 1)
    return (doc, k), value

"""Layer 15 MLP neuron 1674 (component p-82af68dd@100000/layers.15.mlp.down_proj:1674).

The component is almost exactly MLP hidden unit 1674 of layer 15, written out through
the down projection. Its activation is signed and small in most places, and it is
clearly larger in Japanese, Chinese and Korean text, where it tracks the word class
of the current token:

- positive on the endings of verb and adjective predicates (する, した, ない, たい,
  ている, できる, れる ...), the strongest case;
- positive, more weakly, on other content words (nouns, verbs, adjectives written in
  Han characters, kana or hangul);
- negative on function words: particles, copulas, conjunctions and prepositions
  (は, で, も, に, の, 是, 和, 就, 为, 可以 ...);
- negative on the list and clause commas 、 and ，.

Everything else (Latin-script words, digits, other punctuation) is predicted as 0.
The program uses only the current token. It explains only a few percent of the
variance: most of the activation depends on context that a word-class rule cannot see.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping
import re

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

# Verb, adjective and auxiliary endings that complete a predicate.
PREDICATE_ENDINGS = {
    "する", "した", "して", "している", "ている", "ていた", "ない", "なかった",
    "らない", "たい", "る", "た", "った", "れる", "られる", "される", "ること",
    "ます", "できる", "える", "ける", "める", "む", "하는", "할", "하다", "되", "기", "수",
}

# Function words: particles, copulas, conjunctions and prepositions.
FUNCTION_WORDS = {
    "は", "が", "を", "に", "で", "と", "も", "の", "へ", "や", "から", "まで", "より",
    "には", "では", "でも", "にも", "とは",
    "的", "是", "和", "与", "及", "或", "而", "又", "并", "就", "也", "都", "才", "将",
    "为", "為", "对", "在", "从", "以", "于", "可以", "就是", "也是", "都是", "可",
    "有", "了", "着", "过", "은", "에", "에서", "으로", "로", "도", "와", "과",
}

# List and clause commas.
COMMAS = {"、", "，"}

KANA_ONLY = re.compile(r"[぀-ヿ]+")
HAN_OR_HANGUL = re.compile(r"[一-鿿가-힯]")


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip()
    if token in PREDICATE_ENDINGS:
        value = 1.8
    elif token in COMMAS:
        value = -0.7
    elif token in FUNCTION_WORDS:
        value = -0.5
    elif KANA_ONLY.fullmatch(token):
        value = 0.5
    elif HAN_OR_HANGUL.search(token):
        value = 0.25
    else:
        value = 0.0
    return carry, value

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 1675: predicts (almost) no activation.

What the component is: a rank-one piece of the MLP down projection that reads the
MLP hidden state along one direction V (about 33% of it is MLP neuron 15.1675 itself,
the rest is spread thinly over other neurons) and writes along U. Its activation is a
context-dependent number with mean ~0 and std ~0.31 per token.

What we found: no token-level rule predicts it. Token identity, the previous token,
the token's script class, position in the document, and whether the token repeats
earlier text together explain about 1% of its variance or less. Its main part,
neuron 15.1675, is not a token feature either (token identity explains about 2% of
it). So the simplest honest program predicts the component's mean, zero, at every
position. Switching the component off changes the model's output almost not at all.

This program: zero at every position (the first token of a document is exactly 0 in
the data as well).
"""

READS = ()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # The component's activation is not a function of the tokens we can see in a
    # readable way; predict its mean (about 0) everywhere.
    return carry, 0.0

"""Adversative connectives: the component fires where a text turns against what came before.

It responds to contrast and concession words: "but", "however", "though", "although",
"albeit", "nevertheless", and to the self-correction "Wait" (plus the "no" in "Wait, no").
It responds to the same words in other languages (aber, pero, mais, maar, 但是, 但, 不过,
然而, ただし, けど, aunque, doch, jedoch, ですが). Strength is graded: "but" and "however"
are strongest, hedges such as "yet", "hmm", "actually" and "despite" are weak. The word
right after a connective (usually its comma) gets a weak activation too. Every other token
predicts 0, close to the component's typical small negative drift.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

# How strongly each connective activates the component, by its lowercased text.
CONNECTIVES = {
    # strongest: plain clause-joining "but" and "however"
    "but": 3.2, "however": 3.5, "但是": 3.4, "ただし": 4.5, "albeit": 4.5, "maar": 4.5,
    # clear concessions and contrasts, in English and other languages
    "though": 2.2, "although": 2.0, "aunque": 2.7, "pero": 2.9, "但": 2.8, "然而": 2.6,
    "aber": 2.3, "けど": 2.3, "不过": 2.2, "nevertheless": 2.2, "mais": 2.0, "jedoch": 1.6,
    # the self-correction "Wait", and softer hedges
    "wait": 2.3, "hmm": 1.4, "yet": 1.3, "ですが": 1.2, "doch": 1.1, "却": 1.0,
    "actually": 0.9, "despite": 0.7,
}
WAIT_NO = 4.0  # the "no" of "Wait, no", which corrects what came before
AFTER_CONNECTIVE = 0.5  # the next word after a connective, usually its comma


def normalize(token: str) -> str:
    return token.strip().strip(',.;:!?"()—–-“”').lower()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    # carry: the previous token's normalized text and document, so no prefix is re-read.
    word = normalize(prefix.token_strings[-1])
    doc = int(prefix.document_ids[-1])
    before, before_doc = carry if carry is not None else ("", None)
    # The model resets at a new document, so a connective in the last document does not count.
    if before_doc != doc:
        before = ""
    next_carry = (word, doc)
    if word in CONNECTIVES:
        return next_carry, float(CONNECTIVES[word])
    if word == "no" and before == "wait":
        return next_carry, WAIT_NO
    if before in CONNECTIVES:
        return next_carry, AFTER_CONNECTIVE
    return next_carry, 0.0

"""Explanation of layers.15.mlp.down_proj:1677, a near-inert rank-one piece of layer 15's MLP output.

What it does: this component's activation is a scalar per token with mean about -0.05 and
spread about 0.31, and nothing simple in the text predicts it. The token identity, the previous
token, the position in the document, and simple classes (punctuation, digits, words, non-ASCII,
newlines) each explain under 2% of its variance. The one regular fact is that the first token of
each document (and of each packed row) gets an activation of about -0.007 with almost no spread.

So this program predicts the average value everywhere, and the average at a document's first
token. It does not explain the component's variation: on eval its variance explained is about 0,
and its effect on the model's next-token output is the same as switching the component off
(kl_fraction 0.97).
"""

READS = ()

TYPICAL = -0.05
FIRST_TOKEN = -0.007


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    first = prefix.position == 0 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    return carry, (FIRST_TOKEN if first else TYPICAL)

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 1679: a diffuse, near-inert direction.

What it is: component 1679 reads the MLP hidden vector (6144 SwiGLU units) through a
dense read direction V_c (its weight is spread over thousands of units; the largest
single entry is 0.09, and the top 200 units hold only a third of its energy), and writes
along U_c with norm 0.75. Its activation is that projection, times ||U_c||.

What we found (on ~130k training tokens):
- It is switched off by CI almost everywhere (CI ~5e-8; never above 0.1 in 10M tokens),
  and zeroing it changes the model's output by almost nothing (KL ~1e-6 nats).
- Its activation has mean ~ -0.01 and std ~0.26, sign flipping across tokens.

of a document (offset 1, where the document starts within the packed row) and about
0 everywhere else. Its token-level and context-level structure is otherwise
unexplained, so every other position is predicted as 0.
"""

READS = ()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # carry: (tokens seen in the current document) or None at the row start
    n = 0 if carry is None else carry
    doc = prefix.document_ids
    if len(doc) >= 2 and doc[-1] != doc[-2]:
        n = 0
    if len(doc) == 1:
        n = 0
    n += 1
    value = -0.17 if n == 2 else 0.0
    return n, value

"""Layer 15 MLP unit 1692 (the down_proj component 1692) as a copy-run detector.

What it tracks: whether the text is currently copying an earlier stretch of the same
document, token by token, the way an induction pattern does. A copy starts when the last
two tokens have occurred before in the document; it then continues as long as each new
token matches the token that followed the copied spot. The component rises with how long
the copy has run (saturating after 32 tokens), about twice as fast when the copied token
is a word as when it is punctuation, a digit or whitespace. On fresh text it sits near zero.

Why: this unit is mostly active on verbatim repetition of earlier text, and its value
grows with the length of the repeated run. Token identity alone explains almost nothing.
"""

READS = ()

BASE = 0.1  # value on fresh text, where no copy is running
PER_TOKEN = 0.06  # added per token of copy run so far (doubled for word tokens)
COPY_CAP = 32  # runs longer than this add nothing more


def is_word(token_string):
    return token_string.strip().isalpha()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # carry: (bigram -> last position where it ended, position the copy is aligned to, run length)
    ids = prefix.token_ids
    t = prefix.position
    if t == 0 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]:
        seen, ptr, run = {}, None, 0  # a new document: nothing earlier to copy from
    else:
        seen, ptr, run = carry
    if t == 0:
        return (seen, None, 0), BASE
    cur = ids[-1]
    if ptr is not None and ids[ptr + 1] == cur:
        ptr, run = ptr + 1, run + 1  # the copy goes on
    else:
        ptr, run = None, 0
        if (ids[-2], cur) in seen:  # start a copy from the last time this bigram occurred
            ptr, run = seen[(ids[-2], cur)], 1
    seen[(ids[-2], cur)] = t
    weight = 2 if is_word(prefix.token_strings[-1]) else 1
    return (seen, ptr, run), BASE + PER_TOKEN * min(run, COPY_CAP) * weight

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 1693: a diffuse signal with no simple prefix rule.

What the component is. It reads the layer-15 MLP hidden state, mostly through hidden units 1693
and 3006 (unit 1693 alone explains about 12% of its activation). Read through the unembedding,
its output direction lifts tokens such as "config", "computer" and "stones" and pushes down
hedging adverbs such as "supposedly", "apparently" and "allegedly". Its activation is zero-centred
noise, mean -0.03 and standard deviation 0.25, and it fires on essentially no tokens by its own
causal-importance measure. Its effect on the model is negligible: switching it off changes the
next-token distribution by about 1e-6 nats per position.

What this program does. It predicts the component's typical value, -0.032, at every token, and 0
at the first token of each document, where the component is silent (its activation there is
about 0). No rule a reader can state from the prefix does better: token identity, the previous
token, position in the document, repeated tokens and being inside an assistant turn together
explain under 1% of its variance on training rows. A table of per-token means explains about 2%,
at the cost of a long list with no concept behind it.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

TYPICAL = -0.032
"""The component's mean activation over ordinary tokens."""


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    # A document starts at the row's first token and wherever the document label changes.
    starts_document = prefix.position == 0 or prefix.document_ids[-2] != prefix.document_ids[-1]
    return carry, 0.0 if starts_document else TYPICAL

"""Weak lexical predictor for a diffuse layer-15 MLP neuron (down_proj unit 1694).

The unit's output pushes the next token toward words like "potential", "search",
"candidates", "possible". It is switched on, weakly and noisily, by words about searching,
finding, identifying or matching candidates: it is most active on such a word itself and a
little after it. Everywhere else it sits near zero with noise that no simple rule captures.

The program predicts a baseline value, raised when the current token is a search-type word,
and raised a little when the previous token (same document) is one.
"""
from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

SEARCH_WORDS = frozenset(
    """search searching searched searches look looking seek seeking find finding
    identify identifying detect detection explore discover discovery candidate candidates
    potential possible possibility interested dating grep chance considering asking
    match matching meet pairs""".split()
)
BASELINE = -0.03
ON_WORD = 0.6
AFTER_WORD = 0.2


def _word(token: str) -> str:
    return token.strip().lower()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    value = BASELINE
    if _word(prefix.token_strings[-1]) in SEARCH_WORDS:
        value += ON_WORD
    same_doc = len(prefix.token_ids) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if same_doc and _word(prefix.token_strings[-2]) in SEARCH_WORDS:
        value += AFTER_WORD
    return carry, value

"""Software-name detector for layers.15.mlp.down_proj component 1696.

What it does: the component is quiet on most text but lights up on words that
name software: programming languages (Python, JavaScript, bash, Rust), operating
systems and platforms (Linux, Windows, macOS, Azure, AWS), software products and
frameworks (Excel, React, git, Docker, TensorFlow), and big tech companies
(Microsoft, Google, Apple). Generic technical nouns (api, server, module, config,
build, library) light it up only weakly. Its output direction promotes more
tech names, so it reads as a "we are talking about software" signal.

The program predicts, at each token:
  - a small baseline (the typical activation on ordinary text);
  - a large bump on a named tech token, a small bump on a generic tech word;
  - a bump that decays over the next few tokens (half-life 8), so the signal
    stays up through a run of technical text.

Predictions are in the component's own activation units. The simple concept
explains only a small share of its variance (about 2%): most of its activation
is spread over ordinary tokens with no concept behind it.
"""

READS = ()  # reads no other component

BASELINE = 0.05  # typical activation on ordinary text
NAMED_BUMP = 1.4  # activation on a named software / platform / company token
GENERIC_BUMP = 0.25  # activation on a generic technical word
DENSITY_GAIN = 4.4  # multiplies the decayed share of recent tech tokens
HALF_LIFE = 8.0  # tokens over which the recent-tech share halves

LANGUAGES = set("""python java javascript typescript ruby php perl rust golang swift kotlin
scala haskell lua bash shell powershell matlab fortran cobol pascal dart elixir erlang
clojure julia cpp csharp vba sql html css json xml yaml latex groovy""".split())
PLATFORMS = set("""linux unix windows macos mac ios android ubuntu debian fedora centos kali
azure aws gcp heroku unity wordpress chrome firefox safari""".split())
COMPANIES = set("""google apple microsoft amazon facebook twitter github gitlab oracle ibm
intel nvidia""".split())
PRODUCTS = set("""excel outlook npm node react angular vue django flask rails spring laravel
jquery express git svn maven gradle webpack jest pytest junit eclipse intellij vscode vim emacs
jupyter pandas numpy tensorflow pytorch docker kubernetes mysql postgres mongodb redis sqlite
kafka nginx apache cargo pip yarn babel eslint""".split())
GENERIC = set("""api sdk cli server database library framework plugin module package repository
repo config software runtime engine debug debugger build compiler interpreter code tools tool
browser app application program programming script scripts""".split())
NAMED = LANGUAGES | PLATFORMS | COMPANIES | PRODUCTS


def tech_word(token_string):
    """The token lowercased and stripped of spaces and underscores, if it is a tech word."""
    return token_string.strip().lower().strip("_. ")


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # carry: (document label, decayed share of recent tech tokens) or None at a row's start
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    share = 0.0
    if carry is not None and carry[0] == doc:
        share = carry[1]
    word = tech_word(prefix.token_strings[-1])
    named = 1.0 if word in NAMED else 0.0
    generic = 1.0 if word in GENERIC else 0.0
    decay = 0.5 ** (1.0 / HALF_LIFE)
    share = share * decay + (named + generic) * (1.0 - decay)
    value = BASELINE + NAMED_BUMP * named + GENERIC_BUMP * generic + DENSITY_GAIN * share
    return (doc, share), value

"""Layer-15 MLP down_proj component 1697: a weak, mostly unexplained signal.

Over training text the component's activation averages about +0.05 with spread 0.3,
and no single concept accounts for it. Two simple things carry a little of it:

  * Common English words run high and rare or technical ones run low: a space-led
    word's activation rises with its word frequency (wordfreq's Zipf scale), and
    bare word pieces, newlines and punctuation sit below the average.
  * Position in the document: the first token is near zero, the second clearly negative.

The rest is predicted as the average. Switching the component off barely changes the
model, so this only explains a few percent of its variance. Carry: the position
within the current document.
"""
import regex
import wordfreq

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

BASE = 0.046  # average activation


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:
        pos = 0
    else:
        pos = carry[1] + 1

    s = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if regex.fullmatch(r" [A-Za-z]+", s):
        zipf = wordfreq.zipf_frequency(s.strip().lower(), "en")
        form = -0.092 + 0.025 * zipf  # space-led English word
    elif regex.fullmatch(r"[A-Za-z]+", s):
        zipf = wordfreq.zipf_frequency(s.lower(), "en")
        form = -0.059 + 0.004 * zipf  # bare word piece
    elif "\n" in s:
        form = -0.088  # newline
    elif regex.fullmatch(r"\s?[^\w\s]+", s):
        form = -0.031  # punctuation
    else:
        form = 0.0

    place = {0: -0.029, 1: -0.086}.get(pos, 0.0)  # first and second token of a document
    return (doc, pos), BASE + form + place

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj component 1698: a near-silent, context-driven readout.

What the component is: its activation is (MLP hidden vector) . V_c * ||U_c||. Almost all of
it comes from one hidden unit of layer 15's MLP (unit 1698, correlation 0.51), and that unit
has no readable trigger: it is not predicted by the current token, the previous token, the
token's character class, or the position in the text. The component almost never matters
(causal importance never passes 0.1), so the best readable model is a near-constant.

What this program does: it tracks where each document starts (document labels change, and
the model resets there too). The first token of a document gives a value near 0; the second
token gives a small positive value (the only consistent pattern found); every later token
gets the component's typical slightly negative value.
"""

READS = ()

START_VALUE = -0.007  # first token of a document: the component is essentially 0 there
SECOND_VALUE = 0.16  # second token of a document: a small positive bump
REST_VALUE = -0.035  # all later tokens: the typical (mildly negative) level


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """Carry (document label, tokens since that document began) across positions."""
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:
        seen = 0  # this token is the first of its document
    else:
        seen = carry[1] + 1
    if seen == 0:
        value = START_VALUE
    elif seen == 1:
        value = SECOND_VALUE
    else:
        value = REST_VALUE
    return (doc, seen), value

"""Layer 15 MLP hidden unit 1699, the unit behind down_proj component 1699.

What it is: one SwiGLU hidden unit. Its activation is near 0 on most tokens,
with heavy tails (positive spikes up to about 30, negative down to about -11).
Its gate reads user questions and requests (?, "I want", my, help, code),
so it is largest in magnitude there, but the sign of its output varies from
context to context and is not set by the token alone.

What this program does: a short table of token classes, all else 0.
  - chat-template role markers (assistant, user, <|im_end|>, and the tool
    and think tags) predict a positive activation. "assistant" is positive
    in almost every case;
  - first-person request words (I, my, want, need, write, code) predict a
    smaller positive activation;
  - code and math punctuation predicts a slight negative activation.
The values are rounded class means over 4.2M training tokens. The program is
a rough description: it explains only a very small share of the variance.
"""
import re

CHAT_MARKER = re.compile(r"<\|im_|</?tool_response>|</?think>")
CHAT_ROLE = {"user", "assistant"}
REQUEST_WORD = {"I", "my", "My", "me", "want", "need", "write", "code", "make", "create"}
CODE_PUNCT = re.compile(r"^[\s(){}\[\];,=<>+\-*/&|:!.'\"`\\_$^#@%~?]+$")

READS = ()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    word = token.strip()
    if CHAT_MARKER.search(token) or word in CHAT_ROLE:
        return carry, 0.5
    if word in REQUEST_WORD:
        return carry, 0.2
    if CODE_PUNCT.match(token):
        return carry, -0.02
    return carry, 0.0

"""Layer 15 MLP hidden unit 1700. The component is this unit: its activation is about 1.46 x it.

The unit is quiet almost everywhere. Its large values come in two kinds of text that repeat
across the web:

- open-source licence and warranty wording ("WITHOUT WARRANTIES", "the License", "LIABLE",
  "distributed under", "Permission is hereby granted"): it goes negative;
- forum signature blocks ("Joined:", "Posts:", "Kudos", "Follow", "Show Tags", "Math Expert"):
  it goes negative too.

Everywhere else it is near zero. The sign is not reliable: inside these genres the value is
negative on average, but single tokens often flip sign, and the big values are sparse. So this
program only predicts the average tendency, a fixed negative value on the tokens of such text,
and explains about 1-2% of the variance. It looks at the last ~60 characters of the current
document (reset at each document start) and matches those patterns.
"""

import re

READS = ()

LICENCE_WORDS = re.compile(
    r"WARRANTIES|WARRANTY|WITHOUT|LIABLE|LIABILITY|NO EVENT|OTHERWISE|licenses?\b|License"
    r"|LICENSE|[Pp]ermission|distributed under|SOFTWARE|Software|provided|PROVIDED"
    r"|[Cc]opyright|COPYRIGHT|CONDITIONS|limitation|Redistribution"
)
FORUM_SIGNATURE = re.compile(
    r"Joined:|Posts:|Kudos|Follow(ers)?:|Show Tags|Hide Tags|Math Expert|Director\n|Intern\n"
)
LICENCE_VALUE = -1.0
FORUM_VALUE = -3.0


def recent_text(prefix, chars=60):
    """The last `chars` characters of the current document, as the model reads them."""
    last_doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    text = ""
    for i in range(len(prefix.token_strings) - 1, -1, -1):
        if prefix.document_ids[i] != last_doc:
            break
        text = prefix.token_strings[i] + text
        if len(text) >= chars:
            break
    return text


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    text = recent_text(prefix)
    if FORUM_SIGNATURE.search(text):
        return carry, FORUM_VALUE
    if LICENCE_WORDS.search(text):
        return carry, LICENCE_VALUE
    return carry, 0.0

"""Unfinished-word detector for component 1701 of layers.15.mlp.down_proj.

What it does: this component is active on the middle of a word that has not
ended yet. Its strongest cases are stems and early pieces of inflected words
(Russian "связ" of "связанный", "наход" of "находящиеся", "ящ" of "ящийся", French
"ée"-stems, Spanish "-ado" stems), where the next token will be a suffix. It is
near zero on finished words, on suffix pieces that end a word, on punctuation
and on spaces.

How the program sees it: it rebuilds the word that the newest token ends (the
letters from the word's first piece, back to the last space, punctuation or
document start). If that word is not a common word itself, but is the start of a
longer common word in one of several languages, the word is unfinished. Then it
predicts a value that grows with the length of the unfinished word so far (up to
seven letters) and is negative for the first couple of letters. Anything else
predicts 0.
"""

import bisect
import functools

import regex
import wordfreq

READS = ()

LANGS = (
    "en", "de", "fr", "es", "it", "pt", "nl", "pl", "ru", "uk", "cs", "el", "sv",
)
"""Languages whose common words say what a finished word looks like."""

TOP_WORDS = 20000
"""How many of each language's most common words count as words."""

LENGTH_CAP = 7
"""Beyond this many letters, a longer unfinished word predicts no more."""


@functools.lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def common_words():
    """Each language's common words, sorted, and all of them as one set."""
    lists = []
    everything = set()
    for lang in LANGS:
        words = sorted({w.lower() for w in wordfreq.top_n_list(lang, TOP_WORDS)})
        lists.append(words)
        everything.update(words)
    return tuple(lists), frozenset(everything)


def begins_longer_word(stem):
    """Whether some common word starts with `stem` and is longer than it."""
    lists, _ = common_words()
    for words in lists:
        j = bisect.bisect_left(words, stem)
        while j < len(words) and words[j].startswith(stem):
            if len(words[j]) > len(stem):
                return True
            j += 1
    return False


def word_so_far(prefix):
    """The letters of the word the newest token ends, from its first piece on."""
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    pieces = []
    for i in range(len(prefix.token_ids) - 1, -1, -1):
        if prefix.document_ids[i] != doc:
            break
        text = prefix.token_bytes[i].decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
        core = text.lstrip(" ")
        if not regex.fullmatch(r"[\p{L}�]+", core):
            break
        pieces.append(prefix.token_bytes[i])
        if text.startswith(" "):
            break
    word = b"".join(reversed(pieces)).decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
    return word.lstrip(" ").lower()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    word = word_so_far(prefix)
    if not word or word in common_words()[1] or not begins_longer_word(word):
        return carry, 0.0
    return carry, min(len(word), LENGTH_CAP) - 1.5

What the component does: it adds a small, diffuse signal to the residual stream
(its contribution is ~0.5% of the site's output RMS). Its activation has mean
~0.063 and std ~0.34, and is positive about 60% of the time. It has no clear

  - Token identity explains only ~3% of its variance even with a full

MEAN_ACTIVATION = 0.063

The component's activation is the output of one MLP hidden unit, and it is almost unrelated
to the surface text: the average value per token identity explains about 2% of its variance,

"""Component layers.15.mlp.down_proj:1704 (MLP hidden unit 1704 of layer 15, read through its
down_proj column).

What the component is: its activation is almost entirely that one MLP hidden unit (it reads
unit 1704 with weight 0.75 of its 1.19 norm, the rest is spread thinly), scaled by the
unit's output-column norm. Its output direction, read against the vocabulary, pushes
toward additive continuations ("+", "plus", "minus", "multiplied") when the activation is
negative. So it is an "arithmetic continuation" unit: it goes negative where a sum or
product is likely to come next, most strongly right after a closing bracket or a number
or variable inside a formula, and it goes positive on the operators and opening brackets
themselves.

What this program does: it reads the newest token and predicts the mean activation for
that kind of token, zero at the first token of each document. This is a deliberately
coarse, readable approximation. It explains only about 1% of the variance (held-out), because
the activation is spread over many contexts that no token class captures. Its context-
dependence is real (a linear readout of the layer's MLP input explains about 28%), but that
readout is not a concept a person can read off.

Fitted on 8,192 training rows (about 4.2M positions). Means: operator +0.23, opening
bracket +0.14, closing bracket -0.46, digit-containing -0.08, word -0.01, other -0.03.
"""

import re
from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

MEAN = {
    "operator": 0.23,
    "open": 0.14,
    "close": -0.46,
    "digit": -0.08,
    "word": -0.01,
    "other": -0.03,
}

OPERATOR = re.compile(r"[+\-*/=×÷−^<>]+")
CLOSE = re.compile(r"[)\]}]+")
OPEN = re.compile(r"[(\[{]+")
WORD = re.compile(r"[A-Za-z]+")


def kind(text: str) -> str:
    s = text.strip()
    if OPERATOR.fullmatch(s):
        return "operator"
    if CLOSE.fullmatch(s):
        return "close"
    if OPEN.fullmatch(s):
        return "open"
    if re.search(r"\d", s):
        return "digit"
    if WORD.fullmatch(s):
        return "word"
    return "other"


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    t = prefix.position
    if t == 0 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]:
        return carry, 0.0
    return carry, MEAN[kind(prefix.token_strings[-1])]

"""Layer 15 MLP hidden unit 1705 (component p-82af68dd@100000/layers.15.mlp.down_proj:1705).

What the component is: about three quarters of its input direction's squared norm sits on
MLP hidden unit 1705 of layer 15, so its activation is mostly that unit's value, rescaled.
Its output direction, read through the tied embedding, promotes definitional continuations
("means", "refers to", "是指", "とは"). Its activation is strongest on the last piece of a
technical term or acronym that a text is introducing or defining (e.g. "Mens|uration",
"Zeit|geber", "Secure Sockets Layer (SSL)"), but across the text it is weakly tied to any
token or next-token identity.

What this program does: a hand-written, word-level guess at the unit in human terms. It reads
the text word by word and adds up a few cues (weights fitted by least squares on the training
sample):
  - an ACRONYM-like word (all capitals, e.g. "SSL", "AMQP"): higher,
  - a term of 4+ letters already used earlier in the same document: higher,
  - a later piece of a word split over several tokens (e.g. "ometry" in "Stoichi|ometry"): higher,
  - a very common English word (Zipf frequency 6 or more, e.g. "the", "of", "is"): lower,
  - tokens with no letters (punctuation, digits, spaces): slightly higher.
The first token of each document is 0 and the second is slightly negative, as the unit is
quiet there.

Its limits: the cues are weak. On held-out eval rows this explains about 0.4% of the
variance (correlation 0.06). Most of the unit's activity is diffuse context that no token-level
cue captures. A linear readout of the residual stream entering the MLP (a table of 2048
weights) explains about 21% on held-out training rows, but that is not a readable explanation.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

import regex
from wordfreq import zipf_frequency

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

WEIGHTS = {
    "acronym": 0.05,
    "repeat": 0.056,
    "word_piece": 0.047,
    "common_word": -0.041,
    "non_letter": 0.007,
}

FIRST_TOKEN_OF_DOC = 0.0
SECOND_TOKEN_OF_DOC = -0.1


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry["doc"] != doc:
        carry = {"doc": doc, "pos": 0, "word": "", "pieces": 0, "seen": set()}
    pos = carry["pos"]
    letters = "".join(regex.findall(r"\p{L}", tok))
    starts_new_word = tok[:1] in (" ", "\n", "\t", "\r") or tok == "" or not letters
    if not starts_new_word and carry["pieces"] > 0:
        word = carry["word"] + letters
        pieces = carry["pieces"] + 1
    else:
        word = letters

        if word.lower() in FUNCTION_WORDS:
            return FUNCTION
        pos = wordnet.parts_of_speech(word.lower())
        if pos == {"noun"}:
            return NOUN
        if not pos:
            return UNKNOWN
        return CONTENT
    return UNKNOWN


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """The activation predicted for the newest token."""
    return carry, word_class(prefix.token_strings[-1])

"""Component layers.15.mlp.down_proj:1722 -- a near-dead, diffuse component.

What it does: almost nothing. Its activation is a small, noisy number (mean about
+0.03, std about 0.28) that does not follow any readable concept. It is essentially
zero at the first token of each document (the start of a packed row, or where a new
document begins mid-row), and it is a small diffuse value everywhere else.

What this program predicts: 0 at a document's first token, and the typical mean
value (about 0.027) at every other token. Nothing in the tokens explains its
variation: the token identity explains about 2% of its variance out of sample, and
coarse token classes (letters, digits, punctuation, scripts, whitespace) explain
essentially none. So this program captures the mean level and the document-start
dip, not the fine variation.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

TYPICAL = 0.027  # mean activation away from document starts, measured on training rows


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    t = prefix.position
    starts_document = t == 0 or prefix.document_ids[t] != prefix.document_ids[t - 1]
    return carry, 0.0 if starts_document else TYPICAL

The component's activation is negative on prepositions that introduce a
complement noun phrase ("the value [of] ...", "transferred [to] ...",
"published [by] ..."). It is most negative for "against", "of", "into",
"by" and "from", and weaker for "to", "in", "at" and "like". It is
largest in biographical and news-like phrases where a name or place
usually comes next ("governor [of] Louisiana"). This program predicts
each preposition's average activation and 0 everywhere else. It reads
only the newest token, so it ignores that context.
"""

READS = ()

# Average activation on each preposition (English, plus a few common foreign ones).
PREP_MEAN = {
    " against": -1.9, " of": -1.6, " into": -1.4, " by": -1.4, " from": -1.2,
    " than": -1.2, " about": -1.1, " between": -1.0, " among": -1.0,

    " around": -0.9, " through": -0.9, " within": -0.9, " without": -0.9,
    " for": -0.9, " on": -0.85, " over": -0.8, " under": -0.8, " upon": -0.8,
    " to": -0.7, " at": -0.65, " like": -0.65, " before": -0.6, " until": -0.6,

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj component 1724: a weak, mostly-constant offset.

What it does: its activation is slightly negative on most tokens (about
-0.06 on average), with a spread (std 0.25) that simple rules do not explain.
This program predicts the average value for the kind of token being read,
pushed a little more negative the deeper the token sits inside brackets
(parentheses, square or curly brackets, which are open and not yet closed),
and 0 at the first token of each document.

Why: the component's causal importance is essentially zero everywhere (it
never passes the 0.1 harvest threshold), so switching it off changes the
model's next-token output by almost nothing. Its activation is a
context-dependent readout of the MLP hidden state that follows neither the
token identity nor the position in any simple way: token identity explains
about 2% of its variance on held-out text, and this program about 0.6%.
"""
import unicodedata

# Average activation for each kind of token (measured on training text).
MEAN_BY_KIND = {
    "digit": -0.081,
    "punct": -0.080,
    "space": -0.079,
    "newline": -0.071,
    "word": -0.071,
    "word_sp": -0.051,      # a word that starts with a space: " the", " of"
    "word_other": -0.039,   # non-ASCII words (Chinese, Cyrillic, ...)
    "mixed": -0.103,        # tokens mixing letters with symbols, or other
}
DEPTH_STEP = 0.015  # each open bracket level adds this much negativity
DEPTH_CAP = 5       # ... up to this many levels


def kind(s):
    """The kind of token whose text is s."""
    t = s.strip()
    if s == "":
        return "mixed"
    if not t:
        return "newline" if "\n" in s else "space"
    if t.isdigit():
        return "digit"
    if all(unicodedata.category(c)[0] in "PS" for c in t):
        return "punct"
    if t.isascii() and t.isalpha():
        return "word_sp" if s[0] == " " else "word"
    if t.isalpha():
        return "word_other"
    return "mixed"


READS = ()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    text = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    new_document = len(prefix.document_ids) == 1 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    depth = 0 if new_document else carry  # a new document starts with nothing open
    depth = max(0, depth + sum(text.count(c) for c in "([{") - sum(text.count(c) for c in ")]}"))
    if new_document:
        return depth, 0.0  # the first token of a document: the component is ~0
    return depth, MEAN_BY_KIND[kind(text)] - DEPTH_STEP * min(depth, DEPTH_CAP)

"""Attributive modifiers: the component is high on a word that sits inside a noun phrase
and modifies a head noun that has not come yet.

It reads only the current token and the one before it (reset at each document start).
Values are the mean activations seen on training text, rounded:
- numbers and quantifiers after a determiner, preposition or conjunction: "three" (5.3),
  "these" (4.9), "several", "various", "other", "two" (4.7), "this" (3.8) -> 4.6;
  the same words elsewhere (e.g. "each other", "is new") -> 1.5 for numbers and
  quantifiers in the first list, 1.0 for the second list (this, each, many, such, both,
  those, all, every, own, your, our)
- possessives and "some", "any", "that" (his, its, my, their...) after such a word -> 1.5,
  elsewhere 0.4
- "of" after a quantity noun ("the number of" 3.4, "amount of", "range of", "set of") -> 3.0
- adjectives right after a determiner or preposition ("the new", "of different") -> 1.5,
  other adjectives 0.5 (adjectives found by WordNet)
- digits: a flat 0.4
- nouns, verbs, other function words and punctuation: 0.3 after such a word, else 0.15

Plain reading: the component marks the spot inside a noun phrase where a counted or
modified noun is still to come, most strongly for numbers and quantifiers.
"""
from wordnet import parts_of_speech

READS = ()

NUMBERS = set("one two three four five six seven eight nine ten eleven twelve twenty thirty hundred thousand".split())
HIGH = set("several various these other certain few different next previous remaining additional specified respective desired numerous multiple subsequent another".split())
MID = set("this each many such both those all every own your our".split())
POSS = set("my his her its their some any that".split())
OPENERS = set("the a an of in on at to for with by from into between through and or all these this their its his her our your my some any each every".split())
QTY_NOUNS = set("number amount range set lot couple total sum variety kind type majority percentage".split())
DIGITS = set("0123456789")


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    cur = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    if len(prefix.token_ids) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]:
        prev = prefix.token_strings[-2].strip().lower()
    else:
        prev = "<start>"
    opens = prev in OPENERS
    if cur in NUMBERS or cur in HIGH:
        value = 4.6 if opens else 1.5
    elif cur in MID:
        value = 2.5 if opens else 1.0
    elif cur in POSS:
        value = 1.5 if opens else 0.4
    elif cur in DIGITS:
        value = 0.4
    elif cur == "of" and prev in QTY_NOUNS:
        value = 3.0
    elif cur.isalpha() and "adjective" in parts_of_speech(cur):
        value = 1.5 if opens else 0.5
    else:
        value = 0.3 if opens else 0.15
    return carry, float(value)

"""Layer 15, MLP down_proj, component 1726 (activation = hidden · V_c · ||U_c||).

What the component is: a single read of the layer-15 MLP's hidden units. Its weight
vector puts most of its weight on hidden unit 1726 itself and spreads a long, diffuse
tail over about a thousand other units. Hidden unit 1726 is set by the surrounding
context, not by the current token, so no word-level concept captures it.

What this program does: it predicts the average activation of the current token's
broad class (newline, space, punctuation, digit, word, other). Those class averages are
small, so it explains almost none of the variance. It is the honest summary: the
component is noise-like at the token level.
"""

import re

READS = ()

# Mean activation per token class, measured on training rows.
CLASS_MEAN = {
    "newline": -0.076,
    "space": -0.061,
    "punct": -0.053,
    "digit": -0.025,
    "word": -0.028,
    "other": -0.035,
}


def token_class(text):
    """Broad class of one token, from its text decoded alone."""
    if not text or "�" in text:
        return "other"
    core = text.strip()
    if not core:
        return "newline" if "\n" in text else "space"
    if re.fullmatch(r"\d+", core):
        return "digit"
    if re.fullmatch(r"[A-Za-z]+", core):
        return "word"
    if re.fullmatch(r"[^\w\s]+", core):
        return "punct"
    return "other"


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    return carry, CLASS_MEAN[token_class(prefix.token_strings[-1])]

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 1727.

What it does: this component is mostly diffuse noise. Its activation is about zero in
ordinary text (mean -0.05, spread 0.4), and no word or token class explains more than a
few percent of it. The clearest signal is on words about incentives: the largest
positive values (up to ~20) sit on "incentive", "incentives" and "incentivize", and
moderate values sit on words about reward, penalty, stake, motive and profit, and on
optimisation and equilibrium words. So the program predicts a high value on the
incentive words, a moderate one on that second group, a smaller one on optimisation
words, and the average value everywhere else.

It reads only the newest token and keeps no state.
"""

READS = ()

BASELINE = -0.05
INCENTIVE_VALUE = 5.0
MOTIVE_VALUE = 0.8
OPTIM_VALUE = 0.5

INCENTIVE = ("incentiv", "disincentiv")
MOTIVE = ("reward", "penal", "sanction", "subsid", "motiv", "stake", "payoff", "profit", "temptation")
OPTIM = ("optim", "equilib", "nash", "gradient", "likelihood", "loss")


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    if word.startswith(INCENTIVE):
        value = INCENTIVE_VALUE
    elif word.startswith(MOTIVE):
        value = MOTIVE_VALUE
    elif word.startswith(OPTIM):
        value = OPTIM_VALUE
    else:
        value = BASELINE
    return carry, value
